target_customer: Mobile gamers on iOS and Android who play social online games, monetized by in app purchases (implied by category, not stated)
problem: Mobile games were mostly single player, and LVL6 wanted to bring massively multiplayer online games to phones.
business_model: Free to play mobile games with in app purchases (inferred from category; not stated by a source)

competitors.name: DeNA Mobage (with ngmoco)
competitors.what: Japanese mobile social games platform that launched its first iPhone and iPad games in the US in March 2012

competitors.name: MinoMonsters (Mino Games)
competitors.what: Pokemon inspired mobile game that reached 600,000 downloads

technical_complexity.rationale: Real time multiplayer servers with persistent worlds on 2012 phones and networks was hard for a three person team; a University of Wisconsin paper studied a large mobile MMO's architecture.

defensibility.rationale: A live player base can create network effects, but only after reaching scale; games and mechanics were easily copied by funded studios.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Large mobile publishers acquired or built social games through 2012 (DeNA Mobage, GREE bought OpenFeint and Funzio). No source shows them copying or buying LVL6.

market_need_then: Mobile social gaming was growing fast in 2012 per PocketGamer.biz coverage of DeNA and GREE; there is no source for demand for mobile MMOs specifically.

branding.domain_note: lvl6.com now shows an unrelated trading card app operated by Outlier Collective; how the domain changed hands is not stated.

identity.voice_and_tone: Tagline on YC page: We make mobile MMOs

branding.community_and_virality: No press, community or merch about the brand was found.

brand_strength.rationale: No coverage of the brand found; the name is a gaming term that is hard to say and the domain moved to an unrelated company.

outcome_analysis: LVL6 was a three founder studio making mobile MMOs and was in YC Winter 2012. Dealroom says it was unable to achieve a sustainable long term position and lists it as closed, and YC marks it inactive; however CB Insights shows alive and a directory says acquired, and none of these is confirmed, so the true outcome and cause are not public. The factor listed is a tentative inference from the Dealroom wording.
notes: Sources conflict on status: YC Inactive, Dealroom closed, CB Insights Seed Alive, one directory Acquired. No acquirer found. The $20K round rests on CB Insights alone. YC lists San Francisco in the data and Palo Alto in a search summary. The dedicated outcome search returned only generic mobile MMO pages, so the cause is not public. Dealroom names Age of Chaos as a game; I found no independent source. lvl6.com now belongs to another business.
